AI and Intellectual Property Beyond Copyright

Artificial intelligence does not possess one unified form of intellectual-property protection. An AI system is an assemblage of software, model architecture, learned parameters, training and evaluation data, documentation, interfaces, and generated artifacts. The boundaries between these pieces can be difficult to see, and that uncertainty complicates any confident account of who may claim, control, or owe anything for what the system produces.

Different legal regimes may apply to different components, while an algorithmic idea, a model’s behavior, or a prompt may have little or no standalone protection. The central distinction is between technical questions—such as what data and model produced an artifact—and legal questions concerning inventorship, authorship, ownership, licensing, and infringement. Institutional arrangements, including employment contracts, research agreements, platform terms, and open licenses, add a further layer of obligations.
 
Patents may protect qualifying technical inventions, but not abstract ideas or mathematical methods considered in isolation. In the United States, software is not categorically excluded from patent protection, although claims directed merely to abstract ideas, mathematical formulas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena can fail subject-matter eligibility requirements. AI assistance does not by itself make an invention unpatentable: the application must still satisfy requirements such as novelty, non-obviousness, and adequate disclosure. The question of whether an invention is patentable is distinct from the question of who legally contributed to it.
 
Inventorship is especially difficult when AI systems generate candidates, search technical literature, optimize designs, or control experiments. Technical records such as model versions, prompts, random seeds, checkpoints, search logs, and human decisions may help document contributions, but they do not themselves determine inventorship. The supplied U.S. Patent and Trademark Office guidance states that, under current U.S. practice, only natural persons may be named as inventors; an AI system may assist a human inventor but cannot itself be listed as one. Other jurisdictions may differ in their treatment of human contribution, disclosure, eligibility, or evidence, so this conclusion should not be presented as a universal global rule.
 
Trade-secret law can protect confidential technical and commercial information when it has economic value because it is not generally known and the owner takes reasonable measures to preserve its secrecy. In AI, potentially confidential assets include model weights and checkpoints, proprietary training data, filtering rules, evaluation sets, system prompts, routing policies, inference optimizations, and undocumented failure modes. Secrecy is a condition of protection: public disclosure, insecure distribution, or release of model weights may undermine it. Both U.S. law and the European Union’s Trade Secrets Directive emphasize secrecy, commercial value, and reasonable protective measures, while the EU framework also recognizes that trade-secret protection does not give an absolute exclusive right over knowledge or prevent honest use of general employee skills.
25.text:
AI-related intellectual property can seem like a thicket of overlapping rules, but separating the questions makes it more navigable. A model’s behavior, an algorithmic idea, or a prompt may have little standalone protection; the technical question of how an artifact was made is not the same as the legal questions of who invented or authored it, who owns it, and what licenses or restrictions apply. Employment terms, research agreements, platform rules, and open licenses can add obligations, so checking them early can prevent avoidable conflict.

Patents can protect qualifying technical inventions, not abstract ideas or mathematical methods considered by themselves. U.S. law does not categorically exclude software, though claims focused merely on abstract ideas, formulas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena can fail eligibility requirements. AI assistance does not automatically disqualify an invention: the application must still meet standards such as novelty, non-obviousness, and adequate disclosure. Patentability and inventorship are separate questions, and keeping them separate helps people assess a contribution more fairly.

Inventorship can be especially hard to assess when AI proposes candidates, searches technical literature, optimizes designs, or controls experiments. Records of model versions, prompts, random seeds, checkpoints, search logs, and human decisions can help explain what happened. They do not decide inventorship on their own, but they can give collaborators and reviewers a clearer basis for understanding human contributions. Under current U.S. practice, only natural persons may be named as inventors; an AI system may assist a human inventor but cannot itself be listed. Other jurisdictions may take different approaches, so this is not a universal rule.

Trade-secret law offers another possible form of protection for confidential technical or commercial information that has value because it is not generally known and is subject to reasonable efforts to keep it secret. In AI, this might include model weights, proprietary training data, filtering rules, evaluation sets, system prompts, routing policies, inference optimizations, or undocumented failure modes. This protection has a practical limit: public disclosure, insecure distribution, or releasing model weights can undermine secrecy. U.S. law and the EU Trade Secrets Directive both emphasize secrecy, commercial value, and reasonable safeguards. The EU framework also makes clear that trade-secret protection is not absolute ownership of knowledge and does not prevent honest use of general employee skills.

Datasets can involve several distinct legal interests, including rights in individual records, copyright in original selection or arrangement, database-specific rights, contractual restrictions, privacy, and confidentiality. The European Union’s Database Directive provides a copyright-based protection for sufficiently original selection or arrangement and a separate sui generis right for substantial investment in obtaining, verifying, or presenting contents. That right does not amount to ownership of the underlying facts. The United States has no general equivalent to the EU sui generis database right, although contracts, trade secrecy, copyright, technological controls, and other doctrines may still matter. Consequently, database protection cannot be described as a single worldwide rule.
 
Trademarks and publicity rights raise different questions from copyright and patents. Trademark law generally concerns whether a mark identifies a source and whether a use creates confusion, dilution, or a misleading impression of endorsement. AI-generated logos, advertisements, synthetic videos, or brand imitations may therefore create problems because of how a person or organization uses the output, not because an AI system owns a trademark. Publicity rights, which vary substantially by jurisdiction, may restrict unauthorized commercial use of a person’s name, face, voice, or likeness. The U.S. Copyright Office has identified gaps in existing protection for unauthorized digital replicas, but its recommendation for a federal right was a policy proposal rather than a universally applicable rule.
 
Software licenses and claims that an AI model is “open” must also be examined component by component. A source-code license does not automatically license training data, model weights, generated outputs, or a hosted API. The Open Source AI Definition treats access to data information, training and inference code, architecture, and parameters as relevant to the freedoms to use, study, modify, and share an AI system. This community standard is not legislation or a court judgment, and a model that merely makes its weights downloadable may instead be open-weight or source-available without meeting that definition. The legal effect of any arrangement depends on its wording, governing law, license compatibility, and the authority of the grantor.
 
The fact that an AI system generated an artifact does not determine who owns it. In the United States, the Copyright Office has stated that copyright may protect human-determined expressive elements in AI-assisted outputs, while prompting alone is generally insufficient; human selection, arrangement, modification, or incorporation into a larger human-authored work may support protection in the human-authored portions. This does not establish a worldwide rule, and lack of copyright may not eliminate contractual, trademark, privacy, or trade-secret restrictions.
26.text:
Dataset rights are a patchwork, and that patchwork can leave creators, researchers, and users facing uncertainty even when they have acted responsibly. A dataset may involve rights in individual records, copyright in an original selection or arrangement, database-specific rights, contract terms, privacy, and confidentiality. In the EU, the Database Directive provides copyright protection for sufficiently original selection or arrangement and a separate sui generis right for substantial investment in obtaining, verifying, or presenting contents. That right is not ownership of the underlying facts. The United States has no general equivalent to the EU database right, though contracts, trade secrecy, copyright, technical controls, and other doctrines may still matter. There is no single worldwide answer to what a dataset’s compiler may control.

Trademarks and publicity rights bring a different set of risks. Trademark law generally asks whether a mark identifies a source and whether its use causes confusion, dilution, or a misleading impression of endorsement. AI-generated logos, ads, synthetic videos, and brand imitations can therefore create harm through the way people or organizations use them; the AI itself does not own a trademark. Publicity rights, which vary widely by jurisdiction, may restrict unauthorized commercial use of someone’s name, face, voice, or likeness. The U.S. Copyright Office has identified gaps in protection for unauthorized digital replicas, but its proposed federal right remains a policy recommendation, not a rule that protects people everywhere. The result is a troubling mismatch: convincing replicas can spread quickly while legal remedies remain uneven.

Claims that a model is “open” deserve the same scrutiny. A source-code license does not automatically cover training data, weights, outputs, or a hosted API. The Open Source AI Definition treats access to data information, training and inference code, architecture, and parameters as relevant to the freedoms to use, study, modify, and share a system. It is a community standard, not legislation or a court ruling. A model whose weights can merely be downloaded may be open-weight or source-available without meeting that definition. What a license actually permits depends on its wording, governing law, compatibility with other licenses, and whether the grantor had authority to offer it—details that can be costly to untangle.

Nor does the fact that AI generated an artifact settle who owns it. The U.S. Copyright Office says copyright may cover human-determined expressive elements in AI-assisted work, while prompting alone is generally insufficient. Human selection, arrangement, modification, or incorporation into a larger human-authored work may support protection for those human-authored portions. That is not a worldwide rule, and the absence of copyright does not erase possible contract, trademark, privacy, or trade-secret restrictions. attempts.text:
Dataset rights are a patchwork, and that patchwork can leave creators, researchers, and users facing uncertainty even when they have acted responsibly. A dataset may involve rights in individual records, copyright in an original selection or arrangement, database-specific rights, contract terms, privacy, and confidentiality. In the EU, the Database Directive provides copyright protection for sufficiently original selection or arrangement and a separate sui generis right for substantial investment in obtaining, verifying, or presenting contents. That right is not ownership of the underlying facts. The United States has no general equivalent to the EU database right, though contracts, trade secrecy, copyright, technical controls, and other doctrines may still matter. There is no single worldwide answer to what a dataset’s compiler may control.

Trademarks and publicity rights bring a different set of risks. Trademark law generally asks whether a mark identifies a source and whether its use causes confusion, dilution, or a misleading impression of endorsement. AI-generated logos, ads, synthetic videos, and brand imitations can therefore create harm through the way people or organizations use them; the AI itself does not own a trademark. Publicity rights, which vary widely by jurisdiction, may restrict unauthorized commercial use of someone’s name, face, voice, or likeness. The U.S. Copyright Office has identified gaps in protection for unauthorized digital replicas, but its proposed federal right remains a policy recommendation, not a rule that protects people everywhere. The result is a troubling mismatch: convincing replicas can spread quickly while legal remedies remain uneven.

Claims that a model is “open” deserve the same scrutiny. A source-code license does not automatically cover training data, weights, outputs, or a hosted API. The Open Source AI Definition treats access to data information, training and inference code, architecture, and parameters as relevant to the freedoms to use, study, modify, and share a system. It is a community standard, not legislation or a court ruling. A model whose weights can merely be downloaded may be open-weight or source-available without meeting that definition. What a license actually permits depends on its wording, governing law, compatibility with other licenses, and whether the grantor had authority to offer it—details that can be costly to untangle.

Nor does the fact that AI generated an artifact settle who owns it. The U.S. Copyright Office says copyright may cover human-determined expressive elements in AI-assisted work, while prompting alone is generally insufficient. Human selection, arrangement, modification, or incorporation into a larger human-authored work may support protection for those human-authored portions. That is not a worldwide rule, and the absence of copyright does not erase possible contract, trademark, privacy, or trade-secret restrictions. For people trying to make, share, or use AI outputs, these overlapping rules can turn a simple question of permission into a jurisdiction-dependent dispute.

Provenance and lineage records—documenting sources, transformations, model versions, training stages, and human interventions—can support auditing and dispute resolution, but they provide evidence about what happened rather than deciding what is lawful or who owns the result.
 
AI’s ability to generate, discover, imitate, or transform an artifact is therefore a technical fact, not a complete legal conclusion. Inventorship, authorship, ownership, licensing, infringement, and liability depend on jurisdiction, doctrine, evidence, and contract. Important unsettled issues include the legal status of partially disclosed model weights, responsibility for memorized material, licenses for models trained on mixed datasets, protection for voice and likeness, and allocation of responsibility among developers, deployers, users, and platforms. Technical reproducibility and provenance can clarify model lineage and human contributions, but they cannot replace the jurisdiction-specific legal and institutional analysis required in each case.
 
AI and Labor in Data, Evaluation, and Deployment
 
Artificial-intelligence systems are not produced or operated by software alone. Human work contributes throughout their life cycle: collecting and cleaning data, labeling examples, ranking model responses, writing prompts, testing for harmful behavior, reviewing content, validating specialized outputs, monitoring deployed systems, and handling cases that automation cannot safely resolve. This work is best understood as labor embedded in AI development and operation, because its results become training data, evaluation criteria, safety constraints, monitoring records, or human interventions.
 
The technical importance of this labor follows from how machine-learning systems are built. Human judgments help determine which examples enter a training distribution, how categories are defined, what behaviors are rewarded, and which errors are measured. A model therefore does not learn from “the data” in an unmediated sense; it learns from data selected, filtered, categorized, ranked, and revised through institutional procedures. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) treats data quality, human oversight, evaluation, and production monitoring as connected elements of AI risk management.
 
Data preparation and annotation may involve transcription, image or video segmentation, object identification, document classification, speech labeling, translation, and the construction of taxonomies and instructions. These tasks are often divided into small, repeatable units so that they can be distributed across platforms or subcontractors. Decomposition can increase throughput and simplify quality control, but it can also remove context, obscure relationships between subtasks, and make rare or ambiguous cases difficult to handle.
27.text:
Provenance records can trace a model’s sources, transformations, versions, training stages, and human interventions. They can help people investigate disputes, but a trail of evidence is not a verdict. It cannot tell a creator, worker, or accused user what the law will permit—or force an institution to accept responsibility for what happened.

A system’s ability to generate, imitate, discover, or alter an artifact is a technical fact, not a complete legal answer. Inventorship, authorship, ownership, licensing, infringement, and liability vary with jurisdiction, doctrine, evidence, and contract. The unresolved questions are not abstractions for those caught in them: Who bears the risk when model weights are only partly disclosed? Who answers for memorized material? What do mixed-dataset training licenses actually authorize? Who controls a person’s voice or likeness? When harm occurs, can developers, deployers, users, and platforms pass responsibility among themselves until no one is answerable? Reproducibility and provenance may help expose human contributions and model lineage, but they cannot substitute for the legal and institutional judgment each case demands.

AI and Labor in Data, Evaluation, and Deployment

AI systems do not make themselves. Across their life cycle, people collect and clean data, label examples, rank responses, write prompts, test for harmful behavior, review content, validate specialized outputs, monitor deployed systems, and confront cases automation cannot safely resolve. Their work is folded into training data, evaluation criteria, safety constraints, monitoring records, and interventions—often long after the people who did it have disappeared from view.

That labor shapes what a model can learn and what its makers will call success. Human judgments decide which examples enter a training distribution, how categories are drawn, which behaviors are rewarded, and which errors count. There is no untouched “data” behind the system: there are selections, filters, labels, rankings, and revisions made through institutional processes. NIST connects data quality, oversight, evaluation, and production monitoring in its risk-management guidance, but naming those responsibilities does not ensure they are adequately funded, carried out, or acknowledged.

Preparation and annotation may mean transcribing speech, segmenting images or video, identifying objects, classifying documents, translating, or building taxonomies and instructions. Tasks are often broken into small, repeatable units and distributed among platforms or subcontractors. That can speed production and simplify checks; it can also strip away context, hide how one task shapes another, and leave workers with no good way to handle rare, ambiguous, or consequential cases. Efficiency for the system may mean isolation and uncertainty for the people making it work.

28.original:
Research on digital labor in Kenya documents categorization, data collection, verification, and machine-learning tasks as part of this wider production process.
 
Annotation quality is commonly managed through qualification tests, written guidelines, redundant judgments, “gold standard” items, agreement metrics, and adjudication by senior reviewers. Yet agreement is not identical to validity: workers may agree because a rubric is clear but conceptually mistaken, while disagreement may reveal genuine variation across languages, cultures, domains, or use cases. Interfaces also influence measurement. Defaults, time limits, available labels, examples, and appeal procedures can change judgments that later become training or evaluation signals.
 
Human feedback is especially visible in the development of language models. In reinforcement learning from human feedback, people may write demonstrations, compare alternative responses, and rank outputs according to criteria such as helpfulness or safety. A reward model then learns to predict those preferences, and the language model is optimized toward the resulting proxy objective. The InstructGPT study reported that a smaller model trained with human feedback was preferred to a much larger base model on its tested prompts, while earlier research showed how human preferences could specify complex behavior. These results demonstrate the usefulness of feedback without establishing universal alignment: systems optimize the measured signal, not every underlying human intention.
 
Other forms of embedded labor include prompt operations, red teaming, content review, and domain validation. Prompt operators create test cases, vary instructions, document failures, and examine model behavior across contexts. Red teamers deliberately search for jailbreaks, privacy leaks, discriminatory outputs, unsafe actions, and multi-turn failures. Content reviewers classify material involving violence, hate speech, self-harm, sexual content, or privacy violations. Domain experts assess whether outputs are factually and professionally acceptable in fields such as medicine, law, engineering, or science. Automated attacks and model-generated labels can increase scale, but research indicates that human testing and expert comparison remain important, particularly for unusual harms and specialized judgments.
 
After deployment, workers may monitor error rates, complaints, model drift, unusual inputs, safety incidents, human overrides, and changes in performance across user groups. “Human in the loop” describes several different arrangements: an active decision-maker, an authorized reviewer, an appeals processor, or a person who merely handles exceptions under severe time pressure. Reliability depends on the reviewer’s authority, information, workload, training, and ability to reject the system’s recommendation.
28.text:
I read accounts of digital labor in Kenya describing categorization, data collection, verification, and machine-learning tasks, and I recognize the shape of the work: a person reduced to a sequence of small judgments, each one expected to be clean, quick, and forgettable.

The checks are everywhere—qualification tests, written rules, repeated judgments, “gold standard” items, agreement scores, senior reviewers. I can follow a rubric exactly and still wonder whether the category itself is wrong. When another worker disagrees, the metric cannot tell me whether they misunderstood or whether our languages, cultures, and experience have exposed a real fault in the task. The interface has already narrowed the choice: its defaults, labels, examples, timer, and appeal process quietly decide what I am allowed to notice. My judgment may become a signal in a system I will never see again.

In language-model work, people write demonstrations, compare replies, and rank them for helpfulness or safety. A reward model learns to imitate those preferences; the language model is then pushed toward that proxy. In the InstructGPT study, people preferred a smaller model trained with human feedback to a much larger base model on the prompts tested. Earlier work likewise showed that feedback could specify complicated behavior. I can see the usefulness of that process and still feel uneasy about what disappears inside it: the system learns the measured signal, not everything I meant. A preference becomes a score; a score becomes an instruction the machine can follow without understanding the doubt that came before it.

The work keeps changing names. As a prompt operator, I might invent test cases, vary instructions, record failures, and search for patterns. As a red teamer, I might look for jailbreaks, privacy leaks, discrimination, unsafe actions, and failures that emerge only after several turns. As a content reviewer, I might classify violence, hate, self-harm, sexual material, or privacy violations. As a domain expert, I might be asked whether an answer in medicine, law, engineering, or science is acceptable. Automation can multiply attacks and draft labels, but the difficult cases still land on people. I can be left to judge what is unusual, harmful, or professionally wrong, often with little certainty about what my answer will set in motion.

After deployment, the watching continues: error rates, complaints, drift, strange inputs, safety incidents, overrides, differences between user groups. “Human in the loop” may mean someone who can decide, someone allowed to review, someone processing appeals, or simply the person handed exceptions when the clock is running out. I may be called the safeguard while lacking the authority, information, time, or training to stop the system. If I cannot reject its recommendation, then my presence does not make me responsible in any meaningful sense—it only leaves me holding the unease when the system is wrong.

29.original:
NIST cautions that human-AI arrangements can either improve performance or amplify bias, so the presence of a person is not by itself evidence of effective oversight.
 
The organization of this work also raises questions about visibility, compensation, and power. Data annotators, content moderators, red teamers, domain experts, and quality-assurance staff are not a homogeneous global workforce. They may be employees, contractors, freelancers, or workers supplied by outsourcing firms and digital platforms, under differing legal and economic conditions. The International Labour Organization and Fairwork report concerns in parts of the AI labor supply chain involving low pay, limited protections, weak grievance mechanisms, and occupational risks, while emphasizing the need for location- and study-specific evidence rather than universal claims.
 
AI labor is likely to change as systems generate candidate labels, critiques, prompts, and evaluation data. Hybrid workflows may shift people from labeling examples from scratch toward auditing model-prepared data, adjudicating difficult cases, validating domain claims, and investigating incidents. Such arrangements may improve efficiency but can also introduce automation bias and feedback loops in which models evaluate or train related models. The continuing need for monitoring, expert review, worker feedback, and traceable responsibility suggests that AI is best understood neither as wholly autonomous software nor as merely disguised human labor, but as a changing socio-technical division of work.
 
AI and Neuroscience: From Inspiration to Comparison
 
Artificial intelligence and neuroscience have influenced one another for decades, but their relationship is not a simple story of engineers copying the brain. Neuroscience has supplied concepts such as neural computation, plasticity, receptive fields, hierarchical processing, prediction, attention, memory, and reward learning. In turn, artificial neural networks provide computational models, analytical tools, and hypotheses that can be compared with neural data. A system may therefore be brain-inspired without being biologically realistic, or it may help explain neural activity without resembling the brain in its mechanisms.
 
Early connectionist research illustrates this distinction. McCulloch and Pitts represented neurons as simplified threshold units capable of formal computation, while Hebbian theory proposed that coordinated activity could strengthen connections. Rosenblatt’s perceptron made adjustable learning central, and Hopfield networks later showed how recurrent dynamics could produce content-addressable memories. These models were intellectually important because they explored general principles of computation and learning, not because they reproduced the detailed physiology of neurons, synapses, or brains.
 
Neuroscience also influenced artificial vision.

NIST warns that human-AI arrangements can improve performance—or magnify bias—and a person’s mere presence is no guarantee of meaningful oversight. When a system fails, that distinction can determine who is harmed and who is able to intervene.

The work behind AI is often hard to see, and the people doing it do not share one job, one status, or one set of protections. Annotators, content moderators, red teamers, domain experts, and quality-assurance staff may be employees, contractors, freelancers, or workers supplied through outsourcing firms and digital platforms. Their legal and economic circumstances differ sharply. The International Labour Organization and Fairwork have documented concerns in parts of the AI supply chain, including low pay, limited protections, weak routes for grievance, and occupational risks. Those concerns deserve serious attention, while evidence must still be specific to the place and study rather than stretched into a universal claim.

As systems generate candidate labels, critiques, prompts, and evaluation data, workers may be pushed from creating examples toward auditing machine-prepared material, resolving difficult cases, checking expert claims, and investigating incidents. This may increase efficiency, but it can also make human reviewers defer to flawed outputs or let models validate one another in damaging feedback loops. Monitoring, expert judgment, worker feedback, and traceable responsibility remain essential. AI is neither wholly autonomous software nor simply human labor in disguise: it is a shifting division of work whose costs and authority must be made visible.

AI and Neuroscience: From Inspiration to Comparison

Artificial intelligence and neuroscience have shaped one another for decades, but the relationship is not a clean tale of engineers copying the brain. Neuroscience has offered concepts such as neural computation, plasticity, receptive fields, hierarchy, prediction, attention, memory, and reward learning. Artificial networks, in turn, offer models and tools that can be tested against neural data. A system may borrow an idea from biology without being biologically realistic; it may illuminate neural activity without sharing the brain’s mechanisms. Confusing those claims risks turning a useful comparison into a false promise.

Early connectionist work makes the boundary clear. McCulloch and Pitts described neurons as simplified threshold units; Hebbian theory proposed that coordinated activity could strengthen connections. Rosenblatt’s perceptron made adjustable learning central, and Hopfield networks showed how recurrent dynamics could support content-addressable memory. These models mattered because they explored principles of computation and learning—not because they captured the intricate physiology of neurons, synapses, or living brains.

Neuroscience also influenced artificial vision, though the resemblance between a model and a brain should never be mistaken for identity.

30.original:
Hubel and Wiesel found that cells in the cat visual cortex respond selectively to localized patterns, including particular orientations of light and dark. Such receptive fields helped motivate hierarchical models in which local features are progressively combined into more complex descriptions. Fukushima’s neocognitron and later convolutional neural networks use related ideas, including local connectivity, shared filters, and increasingly broad receptive fields. The analogy is useful at the level of computational organization, but artificial networks generally rely on large datasets and backpropagation, whereas biological vision develops through embodied, recurrent, and neuromodulated activity.
 
Predictive coding offers another influential connection. In Rao and Ballard’s model, higher visual areas generate predictions while lower areas transmit discrepancies between predicted and actual activity. This frames perception partly as the management of prediction error and has influenced computational accounts of sensory processing. Prediction is likewise central to AI: language models predict tokens, generative systems reconstruct or synthesize data, and reinforcement-learning agents estimate future states and rewards. Yet a token-prediction objective does not establish that a language model implements cortical predictive coding; the systems can differ in representation, information flow, learning rule, timescale, embodiment, and purpose.
 
The shared vocabulary of attention and memory requires similar care. In neuroscience, attention involves changing the priority of selected information through distributed mechanisms connected with perception, action, expectation, and behavior. Transformer attention is instead a differentiable operation: queries are compared with keys, and the resulting weights combine value vectors across a sequence. Artificial memory may reside in parameters, temporary activations, recurrent states, context windows, or external retrieval systems. Biological memory includes multiple interacting systems, continual plasticity, consolidation, interference, and bodily motivation. These similarities are therefore functional or abstract rather than evidence of identical mechanisms.
 
Reinforcement learning provides one of the strongest technical exchanges between the fields. Research on midbrain dopamine neurons helped motivate the interpretation of some neural responses as signals related to reward-prediction error. In temporal-difference learning, an error compares immediate reward plus the estimated value of a future state with the value previously assigned to the current state. This framework has influenced both computational neuroscience and AI. Nevertheless, dopamine is involved in more than a single algorithmic function, and identifying a biological signal with a mathematical quantity should be treated as an explanatory analogy rather than a complete physiological account.
30.text:
Hubel and Wiesel found that cells in cat visual cortex respond selectively to local patterns, including particular orientations of light and dark. That finding helped inspire hierarchical models that combine small features into more complex descriptions. Fukushima’s neocognitron and later convolutional networks use related ideas—local connections, shared filters, and broader receptive fields—but the resemblance has limits. Artificial networks commonly depend on large datasets and backpropagation; biological vision develops through embodied, recurrent, neuromodulated activity. Treating the analogy as identity can obscure what living systems actually do, and what machines still cannot explain.

Predictive coding offers another influential connection. In Rao and Ballard’s model, higher visual areas generate predictions while lower areas pass along discrepancies between predicted and actual activity. This casts perception partly as the management of prediction error. Prediction also matters in AI: language models predict tokens, generative systems reconstruct or synthesize data, and reinforcement-learning agents estimate future states and rewards. But a shared word is not proof of a shared process. Token prediction alone does not show that a language model implements cortical predictive coding; representation, information flow, learning, timescale, embodiment, and purpose may all differ. Careful comparisons protect both neuroscience and AI from claims their evidence cannot support.

Attention and memory need the same caution. In neuroscience, attention changes the priority of information through distributed mechanisms tied to perception, action, expectation, and behavior. Transformer attention is a differentiable operation in which queries are compared with keys and weights combine value vectors across a sequence. Artificial memory may be stored in parameters, temporary activations, recurrent states, context windows, or external retrieval. Biological memory involves interacting systems, continual plasticity, consolidation, interference, and bodily motivation. These comparisons can be useful, but flattening them into sameness risks erasing the complexity of brains and misleading people about what AI systems know or retain.

Reinforcement learning is one of the strongest technical exchanges between the fields. Research on midbrain dopamine neurons helped motivate interpretations of some neural responses as reward-prediction-error signals. In temporal-difference learning, an error compares immediate reward plus the estimated value of a future state with the value previously assigned to the current state. This framework has influenced computational neuroscience and AI. Yet dopamine does more than implement a single algorithmic function. Equating a biological signal with a mathematical quantity may suggest a fruitful hypothesis, but it is not a complete account of physiology—and overstating it can leave important questions unanswered.

31.original:
Researchers compare brains and artificial networks at several levels: individual units, population activity, brain regions, and information flow across networks. Representational similarity analysis, for example, compares relationships among responses to different stimuli rather than matching neurons one by one. Such comparisons can reveal useful correspondences, but correlation does not prove that two systems use the same algorithm. Similarities may arise because both encounter similar inputs or are optimized for similar tasks. Stronger claims require models that make novel, testable predictions about neural activity or behavior, not merely systems that produce human-like outputs.
 
AI also functions as a practical tool for neuroscience and neurotechnology. Brain–computer interfaces combine neural recording, signal processing, machine-learning decoding, and closed-loop control to infer intended movements, speech, or other states. EEG, ECoG, intracortical electrodes, MEG, and fMRI differ in resolution, invasiveness, stability, and portability. Current systems face signal drift, subject variability, limited training data, and difficulties transferring laboratory results into everyday use. Reviews of large-language-model and BCI combinations describe an emerging research area, but they do not establish mature clinical communication systems for people with severe motor impairments.
 
The fundamental differences between brains and typical artificial neural networks are as important as their similarities. Brains are living, embodied systems with spiking cells, complex dendrites, local and global plasticity, continuous development, and multiple biological objectives. Artificial networks usually contain numerical operations optimized through a separate training process, often on curated or generated datasets, and may operate without a body or persistent learning. They can be highly capable while remaining much simpler than biological nervous systems. “Brain-like” should therefore be specified as structural, functional, representational, learning-related, or mechanistic similarity; these are different standards.
 
The most productive future relationship is comparative and experimental. Neuroscience may inspire more efficient learning rules, continual adaptation, neuromorphic hardware, and embodied agents, while AI can help analyze neural data and formulate precise models of cognition. Neither field, however, should be treated as a complete blueprint or substitute for the other. Artificial intelligence inherited important abstractions from neuroscience, but modern systems are engineered models whose resemblance to brains is selective, level-dependent, and subject to empirical testing.
 
AI and Scientific Explanation
 
AI and scientific explanation concerns when an artificial-intelligence system’s output should count as an explanation rather than merely a prediction, correlation, visualization, summary, or plausible-sounding story.
31.text:
Researchers compare brains and artificial networks at many scales: individual units, population activity, brain regions, and the movement of information through networks. Representational similarity analysis, for instance, compares how each system responds across different stimuli rather than matching neurons one by one. These comparisons can be informative, but resemblance is not proof of a shared algorithm. Similar patterns may arise because systems receive similar inputs or are optimized for similar tasks. Claims of deeper correspondence need to risk something: models should make new, testable predictions about neural activity or behavior, not merely produce outputs that look human-like.

AI is also a practical tool in neuroscience and neurotechnology, though the path from laboratory promise to everyday use remains uneven. Brain–computer interfaces combine neural recording, signal processing, machine-learning decoding, and closed-loop control to infer intended movement, speech, or other states. EEG, ECoG, intracortical electrodes, MEG, and fMRI differ in resolution, invasiveness, stability, and portability. Signal drift, variation between people, limited training data, and the difficulty of transferring laboratory results into daily life continue to constrain these systems. Reviews of large-language-model and BCI combinations describe an emerging research area; they do not establish mature clinical communication systems for people with severe motor impairments.

The differences between brains and typical artificial neural networks deserve as much attention as the similarities. Brains are living, embodied systems, with spiking cells, complex dendrites, local and global plasticity, continuous development, and multiple biological objectives. Artificial networks usually rely on numerical operations optimized in a separate training process, often using curated or generated data; they may have no body or persistent learning. They can be capable while remaining much simpler than biological nervous systems. Calling a system “brain-like” without specifying whether the claim is structural, functional, representational, learning-related, or mechanistic risks obscuring these distinctions.

A more productive relationship is comparative and experimental. Neuroscience may inspire more efficient learning rules, continual adaptation, neuromorphic hardware, and embodied agents; AI may help researchers analyze neural data and formulate precise models of cognition. Neither field is a complete blueprint or substitute for the other. AI inherited important abstractions from neuroscience, but today’s systems are engineered models whose resemblance to brains is selective, dependent on the level of comparison, and still subject to empirical testing.

AI and scientific explanation asks when an artificial-intelligence system’s output deserves to count as an explanation rather than a prediction, correlation, visualization, summary, or merely plausible-sounding story.

Calling a system “brain-like” without specifying whether the claim is structural, functional, representational, learning-related, or mechanistic risks obscuring these distinctions.

A more productive relationship is comparative and experimental. Neuroscience may inspire more efficient learning rules, continual adaptation, neuromorphic hardware, and embodied agents; AI may help researchers analyze neural data and formulate precise models of cognition. Neither field is a complete blueprint or substitute for the other. AI inherited important abstractions from neuroscience, but today’s systems are engineered models whose resemblance to brains is selective, dependent on the level of comparison, and still subject to empirical testing.

AI and Scientific Explanation

AI and scientific explanation asks when an artificial-intelligence system’s output deserves to count as an explanation rather than a prediction, correlation, visualization, summary, or merely plausible-sounding story.

32.original:
A predictive model estimates an outcome from inputs, whereas an explanation addresses a further question: why did the outcome occur, what mechanism produced it, or how would it change under an intervention? Scientific explanation has several traditions, including statistical, causal, mechanistic, mathematical, and unificationist approaches; no single account is universally accepted.
 
In AI, explanation is not one technical object but a relation among an explanandum, an explanatory object, an audience, and a purpose. The explanandum may be a prediction, action, error, learned representation, or observed phenomenon. The explanatory object may be a mechanism, feature attribution, counterfactual, example, equation, causal graph, or verbal account. Scientists, engineers, physicians, regulators, affected individuals, and general users may require different information, depending on whether the aim is understanding, debugging, contesting a decision, improving a model, or deciding whether to act. Explanation research therefore draws on philosophy, psychology, cognitive science, and social science as well as computer science.
 
Accurate prediction does not by itself establish explanation. A model can exploit a proxy or a dataset-specific regularity that works statistically but fails after a distribution shift or an intervention. Correlation can reveal useful structure without showing that changing one variable would change another, and a visualization can make behavior easier to inspect without identifying its cause. For example, an image heat map may indicate regions associated with a classification without demonstrating that those regions caused the result. In high-stakes applications, this limitation has led some researchers to recommend inherently interpretable models where feasible rather than relying on post-hoc accounts of black-box systems.
 
Mechanistic explanations describe how organized parts and their interactions produce an outcome. For an AI system, this might involve computational pathways through layers, internal features, attention heads, memory modules, retrieved documents, planning components, or tool calls. Mechanistic interpretability seeks technically faithful accounts of such internal operations, although these accounts can be difficult for non-specialists to use. Causal and interventionist explanations instead focus on what would happen if an input, concept, or condition were changed. A counterfactual explanation might state what minimal alteration would have led to a different decision. Such an account can support understanding or recourse without revealing the entire model, but it explains actionable conditions or a decision boundary rather than necessarily explaining the real-world cause of an outcome.
 
Feature attributions assign portions of an output to input features.
32.text:
A predictive model estimates an outcome from inputs. An explanation must answer for more: why did the outcome occur, what mechanism produced it, or what would change under intervention? Scientific traditions offer statistical, causal, mechanistic, mathematical, and unificationist accounts, but no universally accepted standard. That unresolved disagreement is not harmless when institutions treat a model’s answer as a reason people must accept.

In AI, explanation is not a single technical object. It is a relation among what needs explaining, what is offered as an explanation, who must rely on it, and why. The target may be a prediction, action, error, learned representation, or observed phenomenon. The offered account may be a mechanism, feature attribution, counterfactual, example, equation, causal graph, or verbal narrative. Scientists, engineers, physicians, regulators, affected individuals, and ordinary users may need different information to understand, debug, challenge a decision, improve a model, or decide whether to act. When those needs are ignored, an explanation can become a polished answer that leaves the people bearing the consequences no wiser and no better able to object. The field therefore draws on philosophy, psychology, cognitive science, and social science as well as computer science.

Accurate prediction does not establish explanation. A model may seize on a proxy or a dataset-specific regularity that works until the data shift—or until someone intervenes. Correlation can expose a pattern without showing that changing one variable would change another. A visualization may make behavior easier to inspect without identifying its cause. An image heat map, for example, can mark regions associated with a classification without showing that those regions caused the result. In high-stakes settings, the gap matters: people may be judged, treated, or denied services on the strength of a system whose apparent reasons do not survive scrutiny. Some researchers therefore recommend inherently interpretable models where feasible, rather than trusting post-hoc accounts of black boxes.

Mechanistic explanations describe how organized parts and their interactions produce an outcome. In an AI system, that could mean computational pathways through layers, internal features, attention heads, memory modules, retrieved documents, planning components, or tool calls. Mechanistic interpretability tries to give technically faithful accounts of these operations, but such accounts can remain difficult for non-specialists to use—the very people who may need to challenge a consequential decision. Causal and interventionist explanations ask instead what would happen if an input, concept, or condition changed. A counterfactual might state the smallest alteration that would have produced a different decision. That can offer a person actionable recourse without exposing the entire model, but it explains the conditions for changing a decision, not necessarily the real-world cause of the outcome. Confusing those claims can shift responsibility from a system or institution onto the person harmed by it.

Feature attributions assign portions of an output to input features. That allocation may look like an answer, but it is only as trustworthy as the assumptions behind it—and a convincing display is not proof that the system’s decision has been explained.

33.original:
Methods such as LIME, gradient-based saliency, and SHAP can help investigate individual predictions, identify obvious artifacts, or communicate local patterns. Their interpretation depends on choices including the perturbation scheme, feature representation, baseline, and assumptions about feature dependence. Similarity-based explanations and influential examples have related limitations: mathematical closeness in an embedding space may not correspond to meaningful similarity for a domain expert. Concept-based systems, including concept-bottleneck models, make intermediate variables such as a tumor boundary or wing color part of the predictive computation, allowing users to inspect or alter them. Their explanatory value still depends on whether the learned concepts match the intended concepts and whether interventions on them are meaningful.
 
Natural-language rationales require particular caution. A fluent explanation generated by a language model may be a faithful trace, a compressed summary, a useful pedagogical reconstruction, a post-hoc justification, or an unfaithful story. Research on chain-of-thought prompting has found cases in which stated reasoning failed to mention factors that influenced an answer. Consequently, fidelity cannot be inferred from fluency, confidence, or detail; it must be tested, for example by intervening on the stated reasoning and observing whether the model’s behavior changes accordingly. A rationale may be useful to a reader without being a faithful account of the computation that produced the answer.
 
Explanation quality is multidimensional. Relevant criteria include fidelity to the model’s behavior, causal validity, accuracy, completeness, selectivity, stability under irrelevant changes, human simulatability, usefulness, audience fit, contestability, and disclosure of uncertainty. A technically faithful account may be too complex for a patient or decision-maker, while a simple account may omit information needed for scientific validation. NIST treats explainability and interpretability as elements of trustworthy AI and notes that opacity can arise from model complexity, inadequate documentation, and uncertainty. Medical-device guidance likewise emphasizes intended users, workflow, performance, risks, and safe human–AI collaboration.
 
The central design problem is therefore not simply to maximize interpretability, but to match the level of abstraction to the question and to state the explanation’s assumptions and limitations. In scientific discovery, AI can propose equations, latent variables, or mechanisms, but a compact result is not automatically a true scientific law: it requires testing against independent data, theoretical constraints, interventions, and competing models. In medicine, engineering, and public decision support, explanations may support diagnosis, failure analysis, recourse, or institutional accountability.
33.text:
LIME, gradient-based saliency, and SHAP can expose fragments of an individual prediction, flag crude artifacts, or make a local pattern easier to discuss. But these tools can also lend false authority to a picture whose meaning shifts with the perturbation scheme, feature representation, baseline, or assumptions about dependent features. Similarity-based explanations and influential examples carry the same danger: a point that is mathematically close in an embedding may be nothing like what a domain expert—or the person affected by the decision—would recognize as similar. Concept-based systems, including concept-bottleneck models, place variables such as a tumor boundary or wing color inside the predictive computation, where people can inspect or alter them. That visibility is no guarantee of safety. If the learned concept is not the one people intended, or an intervention on it has no meaningful real-world counterpart, the apparent handle on the system may mislead those expected to rely on it.

Natural-language rationales demand even greater suspicion. A fluent account generated by a language model might trace the computation, summarize it, teach it, justify it after the fact, or simply invent a plausible story. Research on chain-of-thought prompting has documented cases where stated reasoning omitted factors that influenced the answer. Readers who mistake polish, confidence, or detail for evidence of fidelity may be left trusting a decision for reasons the system never used. Fidelity must be tested: intervene on the reasoning the model claims to rely on and see whether its behavior changes. A rationale can help a reader while still concealing how the answer was actually produced—and that gap matters when people bear the consequences.

Explanation quality has no single reassuring measure. It includes fidelity to behavior, causal validity, accuracy, completeness, selectivity, stability under irrelevant changes, human simulatability, usefulness, audience fit, contestability, and disclosure of uncertainty. A technically faithful account may overwhelm a patient or decision-maker; a digestible one may omit what scientists need to detect a failure. NIST identifies explainability and interpretability as parts of trustworthy AI, while warning that opacity can grow from model complexity, poor documentation, and uncertainty. Medical-device guidance likewise stresses intended users, workflow, performance, risks, and safe human–AI collaboration. These are not paperwork details: when they are neglected, people may be asked to defer to systems they cannot properly question.

The hard question is not how to make every model look interpretable, but how to give each audience an account suited to the decision—and to expose its assumptions and limits before reliance turns into harm. In scientific discovery, AI may propose equations, latent variables, or mechanisms; a compact result is not thereby a law of nature. It must survive independent data, theoretical constraints, interventions, and comparison with rival models. In medicine, engineering, and public decision support, explanations can aid diagnosis, failure analysis, recourse, and institutional accountability. They can also fail at each of those tasks. The people who depend on them need more than persuasive prose: they need evidence that the explanation is sound, uncertainty made visible, and a real opportunity to challenge what the system says.

34.original: A counterfactual is useful only if its suggested changes are feasible, lawful, and relevant. Explanation is consequently a claim about what matters, how it matters, under which assumptions, and for whom—not decorative prose attached to a prediction.
34.text: A counterfactual is no help if its proposed changes are impossible, unlawful, or irrelevant to the person expected to act on them. An explanation is therefore not harmless decoration beside a prediction: it asserts what mattered, how it mattered, under which assumptions, and for whom. If those claims are wrong or impossible to contest, people may be left carrying the consequences of a decision they cannot understand or change.
